column4: The verse directly stages wealth spent so that people will see it, رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ, then says reminders and injury nullify the charity and leave the spender unable to retain anything earned; it exposes why the boast “I consumed wealth” can itself consume the deed.
It names those who spend their wealth for people’s gaze, رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ, exactly matching the section’s contradiction between courting human sight and ignoring the true Witness.
The worshippers “show off,” يُرَاءُونَ; the same sight-root turns an act ostensibly for God into a performance for its human audience.
As the concrete sequel to 107:6, they withhold even ordinary aid; acclaim-seeking display and refusal of useful giving are thereby shown as one moral scene.
The slanderer is characterized as one who جمع مالا وعدده, gathering wealth and repeatedly counting it; this is the section’s quantity-ledger with no worthy destination.
The wealth-counter “supposes,” يَحْسَبُ, that his wealth makes him last forever, joining counted status to the delusion generated by that counting.

After the garden is ruined, its owner wrings his hands over what he spent on it and says he wishes he had associated no “one,” أَحَدًا, with his Lord; expenditure, loss, and the false human accounting converge in the scene cited by the section.
The companion warns that God may send حُسْبَانًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ upon the garden; the counting-root’s fiery dictionary sense becomes the agent that ends the owner’s confident reckoning.
The man given his record on the wrong side says, مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ; wealth that supported status and speech proves useless at the final account.
His next utterance, هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ, turns the section’s “I destroyed” verb upon his own vanished power.

Qarun credits his treasure to knowledge he possesses, while the same ayah makes God the subject of أَهْلَكَ and recalls stronger peoples He destroyed; self-credit and divine destruction answer one another in a single verse.
The categorical diagnosis كَلَّا إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَيَطْغَىٰ identifies transgression as the outcome of the self-regard enacted by the boasting spender.
The cause is أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ, his seeing himself as self-sufficient; the sight sought from others is displaced by a dangerous self-image.
Hoarded metal is heated in Hell and its owners are told, هَٰذَا مَا كَنَزْتُمْ لِأَنفُسِكُمْ; stored wealth becomes the thing they must taste rather than a reputation they can enjoy.
“Whatever you spend” is known by God; this directly answers the man who imagines no one saw him and relocates the decisive accounting from spectators to divine knowledge.

Disbelievers spend their wealth to obstruct God’s way, after which that spending becomes regret and they are overcome; the verse judges expenditure by its destination and result rather than its amount.

The hypocrites turn both generous voluntary gifts and the poor donor’s limited effort into public ridicule; their speech counts visible quantity, while God condemns the reputation-making commentary around the gifts.
No expenditure, small or large, is left unrecorded; the divine ledger preserves precisely what the boastful man reduces to his own tally.
Those who love to be praised for what they did not do embody reputation severed from deed; the verse makes desired public praise itself part of the culpable scene.
The garden owner tells his companion that he has more wealth and a mightier following, establishing the explicit boast in which possessions are converted into social rank.
Entering his garden while wronging himself, he says he does not think it will ever perish; his spoken supposition supplies the confidence later overturned by the heavenly حُسْبَان.
The question “Do they suppose” links their false reckoning directly to the wealth and sons being supplied to them.
The supposed increase is mistaken for hastened good, but the verse denies that valuation; abundance is not its own favorable account.
It contrasts giving intended to increase within people’s wealth with alms seeking God’s face, whose givers are the true multipliers; human social increase and God’s account are explicitly separated.
Those who spend secretly and openly hope for a trade that will never perish; both modes of visibility are subordinated to a lasting return rather than public notice.
God fully pays and increases their rewards, completing the preceding expenditure scene with the account in which apparent loss becomes enduring gain.
No word is uttered without a ready observer; the boast يَقُولُ is therefore itself witnessed and entered into an account.
The final record omits neither small nor great but has enumerated it all; this exhaustive divine count displaces the man’s selective count of how much wealth he claims to have consumed.
God records what people send ahead and the traces they leave, and everything is enumerated; both the deed and its social aftermath outlast the speaker’s own reputation-led tally.
God will tell people what they did: He counted it although they forgot it, and He witnesses everything; this is the complete divine counterpart to boastful self-accounting.
The verse places guardians over human beings, directly denying the imagined absence of an observer.
Those guardians are noble recorders, turning observation into a written account rather than transient human talk.
They know what people do; the row completes 82:10–11 by attaching the record to actual deeds, including unseen motives and destinations.
The rejoicing man supposed, إِنَّهُ ظَنَّ أَن لَّن يَحُورَ, that he would never return; his worldly confidence is another false reckoning voiced before the account.
The answer is that his Lord was always seeing him, إِنَّ رَبَّهُ كَانَ بِهِ بَصِيرًا; this is an especially close parallel to the question whether the boasting man thinks no one saw him.
Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it; human action returns as something seen even when no audience witnessed it at the time.
Whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will likewise see it, closing the boundary against selective self-presentation.
Worldly life is described as mutual boasting and rivalry in wealth and children before its growth becomes dry debris; public competition and the passing object of pride appear in one image.
When provision is enlarged, the tested human says, “My Lord has honored me”; speech turns possessed abundance into a self-serving verdict on rank.
The same passage identifies an excessive love of wealth, explaining the attachment beneath the nearby claims of honor and the failure to feed.
The miser’s wealth will not avail him when he falls; possession cannot secure the power or standing its owner calculates from it.
Rivalry in increase distracts people; the verse names the social contest in quantities and status that drives the boast of abundant wealth.
The command وَلَا تَمْنُن تَسْتَكْثِرُ forbids giving in a way that seeks increase or counts the gift as great; both established readings directly check the self-magnifying ledger of expenditure.
The command not to claim purity for yourselves is grounded in God’s superior knowledge of who is mindful; self-praise gives way to the judgment of the One who sees.
The command to spend in God’s way is immediately joined to “do not cast yourselves into destruction,” التَّهْلُكَة; the destruction-root marks a boundary between worthy expenditure and ruin.
When asked what should be spent, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler; it replaces a boast about amount with an account of where wealth actually went.
The recipient of the record in his left hand begins to speak; this locates the claims about useless wealth and vanished power in the final public accounting.
He wishes he had never known his حساب, making the divine account he tried to evade the subject of his own speech.
What people send ahead for themselves they will find with God, who sees what they do; the lasting divine deposit reverses expenditure made to be found on people’s tongues.
True righteousness gives loved wealth to named recipients and for freeing people; these concrete destinations show what the boast’s bare quantity leaves unspoken.
The answer to how much to spend is “the surplus,” setting a measured boundary against both miserly retention and self-advertised destruction of everything.
Wealth spent in God’s way is likened to a seed multiplied many times; apparent depletion becomes growth when purpose, rather than publicity, governs the gift.
Those who spend and do not follow it with reminders or injury retain their reward with their Lord; silence after giving preserves what boasting would void.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury; the verse weighs the spender’s tongue together with the transfer of wealth.
Spending for God’s pleasure and inner firmness is pictured as a fruitful elevated garden, reversing the bare rock left by the showy spender in 2:264.
Public alms are permitted, but concealing them and giving to the poor is better; the verse supplies the precise visibility boundary missing from ostentation.
Good spending is for the givers themselves when they spend seeking God’s face, and it is fully repaid; this states the opposite audience and account from purchased human praise.

The genuinely needy are mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not beg importunately, while God knows every expenditure; their restrained mouths reverse the dictionary scene of repeated requests and remove spectators from the final judgment.
Spending by night and day, secretly and openly, receives its reward with God; visibility changes, but the true audience and account do not.
Righteousness requires spending from what one loves, and God knows whatever is spent; valued sacrifice and divine knowledge replace claimed quantity.
The verse asks what harm there would be in faith and spending from God’s provision, then says God knows them; it directly reverses the motive and imagined unseenness of 4:38.

Some Bedouins count what they spend as nearness to God and as a means to the Messenger’s prayers; this is the positive “credit with God” sense of the counting-root opposed to 9:98’s loss-led reckoning.
Even spending everything on earth could not have joined the believers’ hearts, but God joined them; sheer amount cannot purchase the human attachment the boaster seeks.

A person given good provision spends from it secretly and openly, and the comparison ends with praise belonging to God; provision, expenditure, visibility, and rightful praise are kept in their proper places.
The relative, needy person, and traveler receive their due, followed by a ban on squandering; purposeful giving is distinguished from mere consumption of wealth.
When one lacks the means to give, the command is to speak a gentle word; the tongue serves the petitioner without manufacturing praise for the speaker.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended completely and left empty; the image gives a practical limit to both withholding and boastful self-exhaustion.
God grants Abraham and his family a lofty “tongue of truth,” لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ; enduring good mention is bestowed by God rather than bought through display.
God appoints affection for those who believe and do right; the favorable place among people comes as a divine gift, not a reputation engineered by spending.
People who give what they give while their hearts fear their return to their Lord reverse the complacent confidence of the boasting giver.
The servants’ spending is neither extravagant nor stingy but stands between the two; the verse supplies the moral measure absent from a tally of wealth “destroyed.”
Abraham asks his Lord to grant him a truthful tongue among later people; he seeks good remembrance from God instead of producing it through self-praising speech.
Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him, do good, and avoid corruption; the counsel gives his treasure the destination his self-crediting account suppresses.
People of knowledge answer the crowd dazzled by Qarun that God’s reward is better; they replace visible wealth and acclaim with the lasting valuation.
Neither wealth nor children bring anyone near to God; faith and good action, not displayed abundance, receive multiplied recompense.
God promises reward and does not ask people for all their wealth; divine demand is distinguished from the human petitioner who can exhaust a finite owner.
If people were pressed for all their wealth, they would grow stingy and their resentment would emerge; the verse explicitly recognizes the limit behind the dictionary scene of repeated asking.
Those called to spend in God’s way harm only themselves by withholding, while God remains rich and humans needy; true giving is framed by dependence on God rather than reputation among people.
A recognized right in their wealth belongs to the asker and the deprived; many mouths become rightful recipients rather than an audience for a boast.
Everyone in the heavens and earth asks God, yet His giving is perpetually renewed; divine inexhaustibility forms the boundary to the human owner depleted by repeated requests.
The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite their own need; real depletion serves another person and is praised without a self-announced sum.
The command to spend for one’s own ultimate good is joined to resistance to the soul’s greed; the real beneficiary and real obstacle differ from the boastful story.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven; wealth entered in God’s account is gain rather than annihilation.
The prayerful set a known share in their wealth, substituting measured obligation for spectacular, undefined claims of consumption.
That known share is for both the asker and the deprived, naming the mouths and needs that make wealth truly leave the hand.
They feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food; the preceding deed supplies the concrete recipients behind the declaration in 76:9.
The feeders say they seek only God’s face and want neither repayment nor thanks; their speech expressly refuses the social return desired by ostentation.
The first figure gives and remains mindful, beginning the direct opposite of the self-sufficient miser and the self-congratulating spender.
He affirms the best promise, so his giving rests on a valuation beyond the visible loss.
God eases this giver toward ease, showing the outcome of wealth released under the right account.
The mindful person gives his wealth to purify himself; giving has an inward end rather than a public reputation.
No one has a favor with him that is merely being repaid, excluding a human exchange as the motive for his gift.
He acts only seeking the face of his Most High Lord; this supplies the true audience for the gift.
The command not to rebuff the asker directs the mouth toward mercy at the point where another mouth voices need.
The command to speak of the Lord’s favor models rightful proclamation: the tongue credits the Giver rather than advertising the speaker.
Peoples and tribes exist for recognition, while the most honored before God is the most mindful; ancestry and social name cannot be counted into true rank.
Within the showy-charity passage, a fruitful garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is most vulnerable; the image makes the late destruction of a life’s apparent investment visible.
The catalog of worldly attractions includes heaped gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and fields; it situates the dictionary’s herd-wealth inside the larger display of possessed abundance.
What people hoard from God’s bounty will be collared around them; retained property becomes the visible burden of its owner rather than an honor.
Immediately before the showy spenders of 4:38 stand those who are stingy, urge stinginess, and conceal God’s bounty; withholding and display are adjacent corruptions of the same provision.
Wrongdoers hide from people but cannot hide from God, who is with them while they plan displeasing speech; it reverses the boaster’s desire for people’s gaze while likewise neglecting God’s.
Hypocrites stand for prayer lazily and only to be seen by people; the sight-root shows that the same audience corruption can hollow out worship as well as spending.
At harvest, the produce’s due must be given while waste is forbidden; giving and destruction are separated even when abundance is visibly gathered.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s way are warned before 9:35 stages the hoard’s fiery accounting.
Whether the condemned group spends willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted; expenditure as an amount does not establish its worth.
Their spending is rejected because disbelief and unwillingness govern the act; the verse names the inward reason the preceding amount cannot cure.
Some promise God that if given bounty they will give charity and become righteous; speech about future spending is placed under divine scrutiny.
When bounty arrives, they become stingy and turn away, exposing the gap between the public claim in 9:75 and the destination of the wealth.
When the earth takes on adornment and its people think they control it, God’s command reduces it to stubble; possession and confident supposition prove simultaneous and fragile.
Those who seek worldly life and its adornment receive the full yield of their deeds here; a human-facing return can therefore consume the deed’s whole horizon.
For those same people, what they made is void in the Hereafter; this supplies the “becoming null” sense included in the section’s destruction-root.
Shuayb’s people sarcastically defend doing whatever they please with their wealth; their speech shares the boaster’s premise of autonomous control over property.
Believers are told to spend secretly and openly before a day without trade or friendship; both display and deferred human exchange lose their value before the account.
The garden owner doubts the Hour and assumes an even better return if brought back to his Lord; false worldly appraisal expands into false eschatological appraisal.
His companion tells him that on entering the garden he should have credited God and denied independent power; right speech at the sight of wealth would have interrupted the boast.
The warning that the garden’s water may sink beyond recovery describes the concrete loss completed in 18:42.
After the ruin, no human group can help him and he cannot help himself; wealth and social following fail together.
Worldly life is likened to vegetation that flourishes and then becomes wind-scattered debris; possessed abundance passes despite its visible density.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring good deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope; the verse explicitly supplies the lasting counter-ledger.
A disbeliever says he will surely be given wealth and children; confident speech claims future abundance as if it were already credited to him.
The reply asks whether he has looked into the unseen or obtained a covenant, exposing the imagined knowledge beneath his claim.
God will record what he says and extend his punishment; the wealth-claim itself becomes an entry in the divine record.
God inherits what the speaker claimed, and he comes alone; possessions and the social standing attached to them do not accompany him.
Qarun’s treasure keys burden a group of strong men, giving concrete scale to the piled wealth that supports his self-credit in 28:78.
Qarun goes out before his people in his adornment and provokes their envy; wealth is deliberately made visible and converted into public desire.
God causes the earth to swallow Qarun and his home, and no group can help him; the destruction announced in 28:78 reaches the displayed possessor.
The former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that they might also have been swallowed; the crowd’s valuation is corrected after the display disappears.
The affluent say they have more wealth and children and therefore will not be punished; abundance is voiced as both status and immunity.
God expands and restricts provision and replaces whatever is spent; the giver’s real source and replenisher displaces the boast of personal depletion.
When commanded to spend from God’s provision, disbelievers refuse to feed the needy; their speech makes possession an excuse to deny the mouth that asks.
After relief and favor, the human says, “I was given it only because of knowledge”; the wording repeats Qarun’s self-crediting explanation for wealth.
Earlier people said the same, but what they had earned did not avail them; the repeated boast has a repeated failure.
The evils of what those predecessors earned struck them, and the same awaits later wrongdoers; apparent gain returns as liability.
After mercy following hardship, a person says “This is mine,” doubts the Hour, and assumes the best return; possession, speech, and false reckoning reproduce the garden owner’s stance.
Unlimited provision would make people transgress, so God sends it by measure; the verse joins abundance to the self-sufficient transgression diagnosed in 96:6–7.
People are told not to exult in what they are given; possession is denied the self-celebrating speech that turns provision into rank.
The arrogant are also stingy and urge others to stinginess; the verse locates refusal to give beside boastful attachment to what was given.
Wealth and children must not distract from remembrance; possessions become a loss when they redirect attention toward themselves.
The dying person asks for delay to give charity, revealing too late the worthy destination absent from accumulated wealth.
Wealth and children are a test while the great reward is with God; abundance is an examination, not a verdict of honor.
The garden owners whisper that no poor person is to enter that day; their coordinated speech explicitly removes needy mouths from the wealth’s destination.
They set out early, confident in their power to exclude; imagined control accompanies the withholding plan.
Seeing the ruined garden, they first say they have lost their way; their sight cannot immediately comprehend the disappearance of what they counted on.
They then admit that they have been deprived, turning their intended deprivation of the poor back upon themselves.
Hell calls the one who gathered and hoarded, making accumulation and retention the acts that answer to the fire.
The same form لِبَدًا describes a crowd nearly piling around God’s servant; the word’s human heap provides a concrete secondary sense beside the boast’s heaped wealth.
When provision is restricted, the tested human says his Lord has humiliated him; like 89:15, speech falsely converts amount of wealth into personal rank.
The correction begins with failure to honor the orphan, relocating honor from possessed provision to treatment of the vulnerable.
They do not urge one another to feed the poor; both wealth and public speech fail to reach an actual recipient.
They consume inheritance voraciously, showing a genuine destructive consumption of wealth opposed to charitable giving.
The contrary figure is stingy and regards himself as self-sufficient; wealth withheld and a self-sufficient self-image reinforce each other.
He denies the best promise, removing the future account that would make giving intelligible.
He is eased toward hardship, the reverse outcome from the giver’s ease in 92:7.
The human being’s intense love of wealth names the attachment that makes accumulation and boasts about expenditure socially powerful.
What is hidden in breasts will be exposed, so the motive behind visible spending cannot remain behind its public performance.
On that day the Lord is fully informed about them; the hidden motive reaches the divine knower.
People will be questioned about enjoyed blessings; abundance ends in interrogation rather than self-awarded honor.
The wealth-counter will be thrown into the Crusher, overturning his assumption that wealth preserves him.
The Crusher is identified as God’s kindled fire, giving the counted hoard its destructive counter-image.
That fire rises over hearts, reaching the inward calculation and desire for praise behind the visible accumulation.
A man’s wealth and what he earned do not avail him; accumulated means cannot buy escape from the final outcome.
One group explicitly counts its expenditure as a loss and waits for misfortune to strike the believers; the verse supplies the negative reckoning to which 9:99 gives the exact positive counterpart.
The person later described as showing off actively repels the orphan; this identifies whom his visible religion fails to serve.
He does not even urge the feeding of the poor; speech that could direct wealth to need is absent before the surah exposes show and withheld aid.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend a division of wealth, the command is both to provide for them and to speak kindly; hand and tongue jointly serve real recipients.
The sacrificial animals’ flesh and blood do not reach God, but mindfulness does; visible quantity and material transfer are expressly distinguished from what makes the act count with God.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from people; their calculation magnifies what comes to themselves.
When measuring or weighing for others, they diminish it; the paired verses expose a self-serving ledger that counts incoming and outgoing goods by different standards.
The rivalry in increase continues until people visit the graves; death supplies the limit that the quantity contest in 102:1 suppresses.
Secret conversation has value when it directs charity or reconciliation and seeks God’s pleasure; social speech becomes a means of giving rather than self-advertisement.
The Messenger is told to take charity that purifies its owners and to pray for them; purification and divinely authorized reassurance replace praise solicited from spectators.
Those seeking their Lord’s face spend from His provision secretly and openly; the same two visibility modes are governed by a single nonhuman audience.
Sacrificial camels are named among God’s signs, and people are told to eat from them and feed both the reticent and the petitioner; herd-wealth visibly becomes food for actual mouths.
Solomon asks whether the envoys would supply him with wealth and says what God gave him is better; he refuses to let a displayed gift determine his rank.
He returns the gift and warns its senders, rejecting the attempt to purchase favor or reputation through wealth.
Those who leave their beds to call on their Lord also spend from what He provided; hidden devotion and expenditure are joined without a human audience.
No soul knows the hidden delight reserved as recompense for their deeds; the reward is kept outside the public field in which praise is sought.
People are told to spend from that over which God made them successors; delegated possession undercuts the claim that consumed wealth was autonomously one’s own.
A good loan to God is multiplied and receives a noble reward; divine accounting turns apparent depletion into increase.
Charitable men and women who make a good loan to God have it multiplied; the repeated promise makes the lasting return depend on the recipient of the act, not spectators.
The distribution rule prevents wealth from circulating only among the rich and assigns it to named communities; destination, rather than a donor’s quantity, governs the social account.
Whatever good people send ahead they will find with God as something better and greater in reward; the true ledger preserves what leaves the hand.
The giver who seeks only his Lord’s face will finally be satisfied; this completes 92:18–20 with a return received from God rather than from human thanks.
God says He raised the Prophet’s remembrance; elevated public mention is bestowed by God rather than manufactured through a boast.

Givers must spend from the good things they earned and may not select inferior goods they themselves would accept only reluctantly; the quality of what reaches another person matters alongside amount.
Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; the fear of depletion behind withholding is set against the divine account developed through this spending passage.
The wealth and children of disbelievers will not avail them against God; possessed abundance cannot provide the power its owner imagines.
The same formula recurs: neither wealth nor children will avail their owners against God, making worldly means fail at the decisive audience.
Earlier peoples were stronger and had more wealth and children, yet their deeds became void; greater quantities and worldly enjoyment do not survive the account.
Moses identifies Pharaoh’s adornment and wealth as means of misguidance and asks that the wealth be obliterated; displayed riches and their destructive end are specifically joined.
The deeds of disbelievers are like ashes scattered by wind, and they can retain nothing of what they earned; this images the nullity included in the section’s destruction-root.
Squanderers are called brothers of devils; the verse supplies the moral judgment between the command to give rightful dues and the measured hand of 17:29.
Humans would withhold even God’s inexhaustible treasuries for fear of spending them away; the imagined exhaustion of wealth is exposed as a motive for possessiveness.
When revelations are recited, disbelievers ask which party has the better station and finer assembly; public appearance and social company are made into an argument for rank.
God answers that He destroyed generations superior in possessions and outward appearance; the reputation comparison in 19:73 ends in divine destruction.
A disbeliever’s deeds are like a mirage he supposes to be water until he finds God, who pays his account in full; false visual appraisal gives way to the real reckoning.
On the decisive day neither wealth nor children benefit; the assets used to establish rank have no purchasing power in the final scene.
Whatever people are given is worldly enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting; visible possession is explicitly set against duration.
Past peoples were more numerous, stronger, and greater in visible آثار, yet what they earned did not avail them; repeated social superiority ends in repeated failure.
When messengers came, those peoples rejoiced in the knowledge they possessed; the self-crediting claim associated with Qarun reappears as their spoken ground of confidence.

The condemned are told that they exhausted their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them, then receive humiliation for arrogance; present consumption and public pride leave no favorable remainder.
Neither wealth nor children avail their owners against God; the repeated boundary denies worldly means any protective force at the account.
The hypocrites say not to spend on those with the Messenger so that they disperse, although God owns the treasuries; speech directs withheld wealth toward social control rather than need.
The garden owners are introduced as a test when they swear to harvest in the morning; their property becomes the site where confident planning and exclusion will be judged.
They make no exception; whether heard as failing to qualify their plan or to reserve a share, the wording marks the closed certainty behind their intended exclusion.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while they sleep; destruction occurs outside the owners’ sight despite their confidence in controlling the harvest.
By morning the garden is like a dark, stripped field; the wealth meant to be withheld has itself been removed.
The most balanced among them recalls having told the others to glorify God; proper speech would have acknowledged the Giver before the boast of control hardened.
They finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing; the owners’ later words replace confident possession with accountable self-recognition.
God recalls giving the opponent extensive wealth; the wealth behind his demand for more is provision received, not a self-created badge.
Despite extensive wealth and social support, he still covets increase; abundance feeds the count instead of satisfying it.
The warning to defrauders introduces a commercial scene in which quantities are deliberately made to serve the self.
The defrauders do not suppose they will be resurrected; crooked earthly measurement is sustained by a false estimate of the coming account.
Their resurrection is for a tremendous day, giving the self-serving transaction its larger horizon.
On that day humanity stands before the Lord of all worlds; the people whose measures favored themselves face the one impartial audience.
The graves being overturned establishes the final exposure in which the hidden contents of hearts are brought out in 100:10.
After wealth and earnings fail to avail in 111:2, the owner enters a blazing fire; the possessed means end in liability rather than rescue.
